comments.name: Ray Strauss
comments.body:
As the son of an immigrant, I believe America has every right and responsibility to enforce its immigration laws. But the rule of law depends on making careful distinctions, and those distinctions seem to be increasingly blurred as people here under legal R-1 visas and lawful asylum status become caught up in the uncertainty surrounding enforcement. There is a significant difference between someone who entered illegally and someone who entered legally, has faithfully complied with the law, and is waiting on the government to complete its own process.

Strong immigration enforcement and a fair, predictable legal immigration system are not competing values. They depend on one another. We can be both secure and just. In fact, we must be. Once people lose confidence that the law will be applied consistently and predictably, public trust begins to erode. We saw the consequences of that during the pandemic. Let's not repeat that mistake.

comments.body:
Way back in the 1940s, my grandmother cared for her mother, who was only 47 but was dying of a heart defect. At one point my great-grandmother was prescribed a medication that needed to be administered hourly, and my grandmother was up all night with her. She eventually died at home. My grandmother was married and 22 years old at the time. She wasn’t a kid trying to care for a cardiac patient while going to school.

Anyone who thinks this teaches grit and determination well, there’s a cost. My grandmother lived to be 90 and never forgot what her mother’s last hours sounded like. There was nothing romantic about it; there was no “teachable moment” of “personable responsibility”. It was just horrifying and devastating. My grandmother’s experience was 80 years ago now but not much has changed, apparently: when you are poor and your family is sick, the whole burden is on you, and you don’t dare complain because who would you complain to? The bootstraps crowd? You are your only savior.

As an aside, I’d also like to add that when my grandparents had kids, my grandmother had no help from a “post-menopausal female”. Her mother never lived long enough to go through menopause, and my grandfather’s mom was not interested in the kids. My grandparents had to do it all themselves while working full-time during the “golden age of America”. The GOP, which wants us all to go back to that perfect time, doesn’t get that caregiving and childrearing were never easy, particularly for the poor.

comments.name: Mel
comments.body: Overall, it's a symptom of how disconnected families have become. When more families stayed close together, the labor of assisting a sick family member could be spread across multiple people. Now that people often scatter when seeking independence, the burden and cost of coming back to help care for a parent or sibling becomes too high. Family caregiving itself is not problematic, only when it falls disproportionately on one person or on children.

comments.name: FNA
comments.body: It is OUTRAGEOUS that a rich society like ours is failing to subsidize home care for the chronically ill and disabled and is targeting the immigrants who can provide it. Bu it is also offensive for pieces like this one to focus on the plight of family caregivers rather than family care recipients. We've already hear plenty about how hard it is to be  a family caregiver. Let's hear about how hard it is ti be a family care recipient--to be neglected by the larger society and regarded as a burden by your loved ones, including those for whom you provided care in the past.

comments.name: D. Lebedeff
comments.body: This is what happens when only billionaires and the Maralago crowd matter.  The rest of the population deserves nothing meaningful and are left to live subsistence lives.

comments.name: Linda S.
comments.body:
I am now retired, but several times over my working life, I was a private caregiver for seniors with all kinds of conditions and concerns.  It is not an easy job!  At that time, I wasn't making $15/hr.

To think that school children are having to  do this is astonishing.  Truthfully, I never heard of it before.  It seems like there is so little out there in the way of resources for these children.  It's a crime.  What is wrong with our country that we can't put the dollars into helping these kids and their families?

It's time to get serious.  Do we need to keep pouring money into a war in Iran that no one wants?  Are Medicare and Medicaid cutbacks (and perhaps Social Security) really necessary?  And what kind of administration caters only to the rich while the common people suffer?

This is something I am definitely going to write my congressmen about.

comments.name: Linda J.
comments.body:
We as a country have tax dollars to spend on a White House ballroom, a huge arch in Washington, D.C. that will detract from 37 other historical sites,  a war with Iran that we started despite no immediate danger from them, and unneeded ships. But we've cut funds from programs that feed our own citizens and provide them with health insurance and medical care. 

Many illnesses that people suffer from are due to poverty that keeps them from purchasing healthy food and getting medical care at the early stages of isickness. Young children shouldn't be deprived of their childhoods when by paying for adult caregivers with our tax dollars, we could relieve them of this burden.

Why is paying for vanity projects for our President acceptable, but helping poor people isn't? The best word I can think of to describe this situation is disgusting.

comments.name: The Drawl
comments.body: What would have happened if Isabella wasn't there to help care for her parents?

comments.name: Audra
comments.body: The way we ignore and treat caregiving in this country is an atrocity. I will forever lament that Dems couldn't get the Build Back Better law passed, with the bare minimum of improvements. It's nothing but red tape, limited services, low wages / lack of staff that no one should have to navigate, much less kids.

articles.title: The U.S. Relies on Family Caregivers. Millions of Them Are Kids.
articles.summary: The modern health care system requires the work of caregiving to fall to whoever else lives in a household — even if they’re kids.

comments.name: Adam
comments.body: My mother and grandmother were both "stay-at-home" moms, if by "at-home" one means at the foodbank, library, school, cub scouts, retirement home, community center, children's hospital, union office, good shepherd home, meals on wheels, and local fire station; in short, at all the vital unmonetized organizations that once made our society a real civilization, and which are all decayed because industry convinced first men and then women that humans are worthless unless we earn government-issued currency performing tasks for profit-making businesses.

comments.name: From Texas
comments.body: I'm 63. We used to say someone had character, now we discuss their "content." It's so superficial.

comments.name: Brandy
comments.body: I think this is a trend everywhere. I don't think it is any specific content. A lot of millennials have aged out and don't realize it. If one is over 35, youth believes you to be middle-aged even if you aren't quite there yet. I've noticed it on X and Substack and TikTok and Bluesky. I think people have just finally had enough of watching the same old stuff in a different package every day. We are basically living the same scare tactics from both sides of every topic and have been for 11 years or so. It's boring.

comments.name: Megan
comments.body:
I don’t know who any of these people are, but as the current admin rolls back safeguards and oversight of our food production systems, there is absolutely nothing conservative coded about having a garden.  

I recognize that growing your own food isn’t an option for everyone, but articles like this one are socially discouraging to anyone who might want a little more control over what they consume. The sentence ‘it’s not cute anymore to be spending hours making Skittles from scratch when so many people can’t even afford haircuts and toilet paper,’ I find particularly insidious.

comments.name: yeahbut
comments.body:
@Eric R.
"We have entire generations of narcissists creating alternative realities and everyday people suffering trying to navigate the real world." 

I wrote my psychology master's thesis on narcissism in american culture waaaay back in 2008, after years of experience with narcissistic personalities in my career, and and much academic  research. (I thought narcissism was a serious problem back Then! Naive right?)

I learned very early on in my experience / research was that one of the fundamental truisms / hallmark traits of the narcissistic personality is the absolute need for attention, good or bad, positive or negative, to keep their fragile ego balloon inflated.

I read and heard more than a few times over the years that  the worst thing you can do to a narcissist is ignore him or her.

comments.name: Carrie
comments.body: Another influencer family I stumbled across by accident one day features a beautiful couple with beautiful children and all they seem to do is move constantly. The wife gets one facial procedure after another, shops all the time and then shows off all her purchases. With the backdrop of what appears to be the messiest home in  America, the two chatter on about the most inane, vacuous topics imaginable. Do they ever read? Pursue lofty goals? What drivel...and they get richer every day. Why? If people stopped watching and buying into the products they sell, they might have to get real jobs. I used to follow them from time to time because in the beginning they were kind of cute, but the magic has been replaced by disgust on my part that nothing ever seems to satisfy them anymore.  So it is with most influencers. Tradwife indeed! Stop following and these people will go away.

comments.name: JZ
comments.body: Hmmm, here's a suggestion: how about people get back to spending more time living their own lives rather than viewing the fake lives of "influencers." Reality, what a concept!

comments.name: LF
comments.body:
I follow Nara Smith on Tik Tok and IG so I’ve seen a lot of her content. I have several issues with this commentary on her but I’ll just focus on a couple of things that are especially egregious. 

1. To say that she regularly wears prairie dresses is laughable. Most of the time Nara is cooking while wearing high fashion. That is the whole point of her videos — over the top recipes done in over the top clothing, low sexy voice included. It’s meant to be fantasy for fun to watch online— no different from Emily in Paris stars in their made for the runway outfits or SJP’s character in SATC, Carrie, living in Manhattan wearing Manolo’s on a freelance writer’s salary. To call Nara out on her content while being okay with the others is a ridiculous double standard.

2. Nara is a Black woman — yes her father is White but she identifies as Black. To write this article about tradwives and use her as the model/lead (not the first time the NY Times has done this) without even acknowledging the history of Black women and domestic work in the United States of America and especially how they have been viewed in the entertainment industry, is a special kind of white privilege playing out in this article. 

3. As a Black woman who sees constant double standards in the work world when it comes to what is accepted and not accepted from Black and White women — I have to wonder — if Nara was white with blue eyes and blonde hair if she would get this much flack from the NY Times.

articles.title: The Tradwife Illusion Meets the Anti-Trump Reality
articles.summary: Nara Smith’s illusion meets the anti-Trump reality.

comments.name: RobW
comments.body: It isn't a victory for the left if we lose the Senate. I'm more attuned to him politically but she had a much better chance of winning in November. I feel we're doomed.

comments.name: TimM.
comments.body: El-Sayed had a 1% win (about 35k votes) over Stevens.  but the 3rd candidate received about 66k votes and she's politically more like Stevens.  The question is - if she hadn't run, would Stevens had won?  That's a moot point for the election but is important when you look at the November election - El-Sayed must pull in voters that normally don't/won't vote DSA.  Will he be able to reach them and respond to their wants?

comments.name: CMC
comments.body:
I read that the Republicans nominate radicals all the time, so what's the problem with nominating El-Sayed? Indeed they do, most notably Ken Paxton in Texas. That is why James Talarico has a chance to flip a reliably Republican seat in the Senate.

Maybe the Bernie Sanders theory is right, that voters will turn out in droves to elect a true progressive like Dr. El-Sayed. I certainly hope so. But what if Bernie is mistaken? In that case all the effort to turn the tables in Texas will go up in smoke in Michigan. The most important thing is that however it turns out, either cocksure moderates or progressives must be willing to admit they were wrong.

comments.name: nom d affichage
comments.body:
The British Labour Party left tried this with Jeremy Corbyn in 2017. It lost. The party was seen as too radical and frightened the middle that might have voted for them to vote right instead and the country was condemned to another right wing Conservative government.

At the moment it seems the Democrats are almost pushing at an open door, but if they lean too left for middle America in the midterms they will likely not take the House or Senate. If they do it in the GE they will lose to whoever replaces Trump. 

You don't win elections by moving the extreme ends, you win it  by moving the middle, with the odd exception of people who decline to vote at elections because they don't consider the leftmost candidate left enough. (Hillary and Kamala anyone?) Every not voting DSA supporter will be another virtual vote Republican.

comments.name: Myra
comments.body: Yes, the race was closer than polling showed, but let's also celebrate the fact that, even though his campaign was hugely outspent by the Stevens campaign, Sayed still won more votes. If the spending had been equal, might he have won by a much higher percent? I think this only illustrate how important it is to get big money OUT of political campaigns. I'm so tired of being stomped on by corporate criminals whose shoes cost more than my annual salary.

comments.name: David Gespass
comments.body: It seems that every time a progressive wins a primary, that progressive becomes, to Republicans, the "most radical" candidate in history, even as the Democratic gerontocracy has consistently moved right, at least since the Clinton presidency. It now remains to be seen whether their "vote blue no matter who" mantra applies when they lose. So far, it's mainly been an unsuccessful attempt to force unhappy potential Democratic voters to hold their noses and vote for lackluster candidates the gerontocracy has anointed.

comments.name: greg
comments.body: point #2....the amount spent to defeat him...squeaker or not, one would assume that that cash advantage, from whatever source, would do the trick.  It did not.  What does that say about the motives for his election, and what does that portend.  Money in, money out....hope vs fear?  I think he will take the Republican out.  This is the Trump playbook on the Dem side, the out of the box candidate for an electorate tired of treading lightly

comments.name: Realist
comments.body:
I fear that the "progressives" in Michigan have thrown away another Senate seat in the last election that may matter. El-Sayed's margin in the primary does not suggest that there will be sufficient support to win over enough unaffiliateds to beat Rogers, backed up by the Trumpers' bucks and bigotry, in the General. I sympathize with those who are tiring of half a loaf. but the alternative may be sociopolitical starvation.

I will be happy to be proven wrong.

articles.title: The Left Wins a Nail-Biter in Michigan: 8 Takeaways From Tuesday’s Primaries
articles.summary: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed narrowly prevailed over Representative Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary for Senate in Michigan, setting up a nervy race to November for the party.

comments.name: Dybee
comments.body: Mr. Stephens tellingly neglects to mention that the same report he cited on Medicare said that Medicare for all would reduce total expenditures on America healthcare, because of healthcare savings.

comments.name: Medford WI
comments.body: Currently, the federal gov and states pay 50% of all health dollars, the other 50% paid by private companies and persons.  A tax spread out among employers and as a VAT/sales tax would raise the 1.5 trillion annual private amount now spent, relieving companies of a huge burden and roping in employers who now do not insure their employees.  Yes, the gov would be spending more but it would also be raising the amount it can spend on health.  There are several ways to raise the money currently paid privately, spreading out the pain, to get us all covered.

comments.name: Bob Briggs
comments.body: Bret is very dishonest when it comes to Medicare for All, because he wails about the headline pricetag without counting the current costs of our medical insurance system, which it would replace.  Medicare for all would be moderately less expensive initially (cutting out billions in administrative overhead), and the savings would ramp up with group negotiations on costs for pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

comments.name: LF
comments.body:
If other countries can have Medicare type health care for all their citizens, mostly much smaller countries with fewer natural resources and far fewer billionaires, then why can't the US?  We're supposed to be one of the richest smartest countries in the world, but according to Bret we can't afford it or figure out how to do it economically?  Other countries have.

We spend nearly twice as much as our peers, don't get as much care or live as long, and unlike other countries have a significant percent of citizens who have no health coverage at all.  We're a well educated country and if can't figure out how to make a health care system work for all, it's because it isn't a priority.  We've no real excuse otherwise.  

As for driving private health care businesses out of business...That word "business" is a big clue as to why Americans pay so much more for their drugs and health care than peers. Our basically federalized (socialized?) military structure certainly hasn't shut down military businesses.  Quite the opposite.  The more health care prices rise, the more government doesn't keep pace, the more private concierge practices are arising.  Don't tell us doctors couldn't figure out how to make more money if that's their goal, even in a public health care system.

comments.name: Rich from Philly
comments.body:
Medicare-for-all critics are quick to point out that it would involve a tax increase, but never mention that the tax increase would be more than offset by no longer having to pay health insurance premiums.
As a Scandinavian acquaintance of mine asks, "Higher taxes give us free healthcare, free university education, subsidized child care and subsidized housing.  You buy everything ala carte on the private market where it's hideously more expensive.  Why?"

comments.name: Johnny Panic
comments.body:
" not to mention an end to most private medical insurance." 

Is that such a bad thing in a time when many people only have access to "insurance" plans that are little more than scams to line the pockets of investors?

comments.name: Don
comments.body: I'd like an explanation of why Medicare-for-all would bankrupt us but countries with universal medical coverage do medicine for much less than we do.  Is Medicare-for-all bad universal coverage or are we not capable of good universal coverage?

comments.name: RH
comments.body: I am pretty worn out by the dishonesty of those who routinely decry the cost of Medicare for All by saying how much it would cost tax payers to fund such a program without acknowledging how much every taxpayer (and nontaxpayer) would save in health insurance premiums no longer needed, uncovered medical expenses now covered, co-pays, deductibles, pre-existing conditions, etc.  That 30 trillion dollar price tag (over a 10 year period) gets to be a lot less when you net it out.  How about it, Bret?

articles.title: Doesn’t Anybody Want to Win This Thing?
articles.summary: Democrats and Republicans are both playing with fire.

comments.name: Andrew Macdonald
comments.body: These are not job producing projects either ultimately. We are really heading backward.

comments.name: Jane Doe
comments.body: I’m confused: why isn’t it possible to use solar-powered systems? I mean, it’s Texas, right? I’ve heard there’s plenty of sunshine.

comments.name: susan
comments.body:
In Loudoun County Virginia (datacenter alley) in early July the gas fired electrical plant built by a data center to serve their own demand, failed and the diesel generators came on to supply power to the facility.  Black smoke from the diesel generators poisoned the air for the neighbors.

Bring your own fossil gas power is a bad idea.  It gets around the climate rules we’ve passed into law in Virginia.  Data centers should be building solar everywhere to meet their energy demand and making their facilities energy efficient.  https://www.wusa9.com/article/news/investigations/vantage-data-center-loudoun-county-air-pollution-piedmont-environmental-council/65-ffa00add-bb5a-4b8b-8873-f28b577c6abe

comments.name: Kathryn
comments.body:
Here in Australia our Prime Minister has just announced that all data centres must be powered by new renewable sources provided by the AI companies. Gas can provide a small fraction of energy needs to firm up when renewables are unable to meet need. This will ensure our power bills do not increase and will contribute to meeting our commitments to reduce carbon emissions. 
What a disaster this Trump regime is for the planet and for local residents near these centres, whose air quality will be horrific!

comments.name: Linda J.
comments.body: When an AI center is built as close to Mar-a-Lago as possible, and another one goes up in Bedminster, NJ near Trump's country club, I'll believe AI centers are essential. I'll also believe that our war in Iran is essential when Barron Trump enlists in the army and volunteers for service there.

comments.name: SA
comments.body: The generators from the firm supplying El Paso Electric aren't even using efficient combined-cycle turbines that utilities have used at scale for more than two decades.  These are simple natural-gas fired piston engines.  They will burn far more gas - and release far more pollution - than necessary.

comments.name: Tamara
comments.body: My air quality started to tank with Trump 2016. Current AQI 161. I am far from the fires. I am assuming this is smoke from Washington and Canada too. We had zero snowpack and El Niño is no longer a boy. The man who implored I inject bleach into my veins is now adding more to my asthma burden. I may never go outside again. I’m too disabled to handle it. I feel awful. Let’s talk about that. You don’t have to be at my level of spine disease to feel the impact. This is not sustainable.

comments.name: Linda Harmon
comments.body: I am shocked no one pointed out the fact that air pollution knows no boundaries. The air belongs to everyone and thus affecting everyone’s right to breathe clean air and save our planet from devastating climate change. This administration is decimating the power of the EPA to act. Anyone involved in AI should be ashamed until their affect on our climate is addressed. I’m so disgusted.

articles.title: Trump’s Vision for A.I. Dominance Comes With Major Air Pollution

comments.name: RB
comments.body: Keep the blue wave going the courts are helping Republicans stay in power by disenfranchising minority voters. Democrats needs to be in control of Congress come November.

comments.name: Dearson
comments.body: Regardless of the name applied to them, progressives are forcing the Democratic Party establishment to not simply grow, but change. The Schumer establishment needs to evolve and behave as the heirs of the New Deal of FDR and the Great Society of LBJ.

comments.name: David--Philly
comments.body:
If history is a lesson, George McGovern of 1972, and Walter Mondale of 1984 were darlings of the base, and none of the third parties tried to run against them as I remember from childhood, and my voting age youth.  McGovern and Mondale were seasoned politicians with no "crazy" ideas. They lost more than 40 states to Nixon and Reagan.  

Most of the DSA and far left candidates are politically green, more talk than action, and outside of a deep blue congressional district, a gift to the Republicans.  I can imagine the joy of Susan Collins, and Mike Rogers of Michigan. 

David Philly

comments.name: Steve Hunter
comments.body: The Democratic establishment has been in power for decades and where are we today, abused by trump, MAGA and indifferent Republican politicians. It is time for a change.

comments.name: DoktorDNA
comments.body: What does Mallory McMorrow get for dropping out of the race a month ago, leaving her name on the ballot and receiving over 60,000 votes? If one in five voters had switched their vote to Stevens, we would be having a very different conversation today. There is a word for that sort of action in popular election culture but I can't quite think of it.

comments.name: Ivermarkt
comments.body:
“This is only the beginning,” Mr. McKinney said in a news release. “Our next chapter starts in January where I will work tirelessly, as I have my whole career, fighting for every resident of my district.”

Oh brother, where have we heard that before?

comments.name: Pearl
comments.body: Finally, the younger generation is rising up. To be expected.  It’s time the old career politicians retire. They are not in-touch with their constituents. As for the old fashioned republicans… bubye

comments.name: ErikW65
comments.body:
Thanks to Mr. Thanedar for his many years of service to our democratic republic, and taking the loss with grace!

It's time for those who benefitted from our conflicted campaign financing system to move on with their lives and make room for those who will allow America to grow into something new.  

Let's start by doing away with any exemptions to the prohibition of foreign agents from acting as lobbyists to members of Congress.

articles.summary: Representative Shri Thanedar is among a wave of Democratic incumbents in Congress whom primary voters have sent packing in a surge of anti-incumbent fervor this cycle.

comments.name: Joshua
comments.body: You have to wonder what percentage of the admin bloat could be streamlined by AI solutions.

comments.name: ValleyGirl
comments.body: No one is entitled to their job. Ridiculing your employer has nothing to do with academic freedom. Oversized ego is the issue here. Badmouthing your employer; forgoing several months of tenure: ego, loud and clear.

comments.name: Steve LaPorte
comments.body: Administrative bloat at universities is, unfortunately, fairly widespread in America.  Typical symptoms are: inflated salaries for university presidents and senior administrators, creation of an increasing number of administrative positions, a decrease in the ratio of dollars spent on instruction vs. dollars spent on administration, a decrease in tenured faculty (through attrition or outright layoffs) in favor of low-paid adjunct faculty on year-by-year contracts, and a decrease in scholarships available to students.  What is completely unexcusable is that these trends are present at an alarmingly large number of public universities, meaning that the taxpayers who support those universities are getting a raw deal.  State legislatures need to pass laws controlling administrative bloat at state-funded universities - and they need to act now.

comments.name: Patrick Pine
comments.body: So glad I was able to go to undergrad and grad school in the 70s - at a well regarded private university in the Pacific Northwest.  I had little money or family support but I worked a lot; received some scholarships and was able to borrow under a federally subsidized loan program paying 3% simple interest.  I left after six years owing about $10,000 which I paid off over the next ten years.  But tuition was around $3000 then - now it is in the $50,000 plus range and loan terms not nearly so favorable.  But that school is working on a merger with another university in the region - in part to reduce administrative overhead.  I hope my alma mater meets a better fate than so many others like the New School.

comments.name: Derek
comments.body: Faculty need to protect themselves by becoming a member of a union, like the AAUP. Faculty should be allowed to collective bargain and protect themselves from their authoritarian administrations, who are more often do not bargain in good faith. Until faculty stand up for themselves through a collective, then there are no protections that will ensure their ability to educate students and conduct research. It is time for university professors to play hardball with their administrations; otherwise, they will continue to be pushed around or worse.

comments.name: Camille
comments.body: I don't understand why a school that is short on funds would pause admissions.

comments.name: Andrea
comments.body:
As noted in the article, higher education relies on adjuncts who receive no benefits, no job protection, and a fraction of the pay given to regular faculty. 
And yet students pay the same tuition for a course taught by an adjunct as one taught by a professor with tenure.
For example, if the adjunct gets $1k/credit hour, and the course costs $1k/credit hour, it takes only one student to pay the adjunct's salary, but there may be 30 - 100 students in that class. 
The university pockets the difference between the adjunct's pay and a full professor's pay. Students and their parents should know that they are subsidizing wage theft that benefits the university. 
We need transparency in tuition so that students and their parents know where their tuition money goes.

comments.name: Pablo96
comments.body:
I hope many, many colleges and universities across the country find themselves in the same situation as New School: recognizing their indulgences (administrators AND educators) have gone too far and the cost of an American education is too high. 

Consider sending your child to a university in the EU or Asia: will learn a new language and get equally as good of an education for better ROI than handing over the bags of money required to get a 4-year university degree in the U.S.

articles.summary: Putin’s barrage kills 17, since Kyiv wasn’t able to intercept the missiles.

comments.name: Dean Graves
comments.body: Wars are fought in the here and now, in the could have, would have, should have.  Ukraine now has no air defense- none, nada, zero and will remain in that condition for years to come, meaning that this war is now a Russian turkey shoot. Zelensky's call for a ceasefire will only come now if he accepts surrender.  If not, Ukraine will cease to exist.

comments.name: d rosenberg
comments.body: Don't worry. Trump asked Putin and Putin told him Russia isn't threatening Ukraine, so all is well.

comments.name: d rosenberg
comments.body: As always, this spiteful and deceitful administration tries to blame Biden, who did the right thing by helping Ukraine.

comments.name: Lyndon Bradish
comments.body:
The Iran war/excusrsion has shown that the American Empire is less of an empire than we thought.

One regional conflict and supplies are seriously depleted.

One real war with a real enemy and America would be left firing handguns at the enemy within weeks.

In the last 10 years the presidents (yes, all of them) have been negligent in ensuring the military is properly supplied. Where has all the money gone??

Some serious and immediate firings are warranted.

comments.name: R Kerr
comments.body: Trump likes to throw people under the bus for his own entertainment. My bet is that Ukraine will not get the defensive weapons they need.

comments.name: Rick C
comments.body:
Even if Democrats were to stop holding the country hostage and fund DoD it will take years to replenish inventories. That is the reality of the supply chain.  

US has no strategic interest in Ukraine. It is a European problem.  They can fund and support Ukraine.  US is not the world cop and needs to give priority to US interests.

comments.name: Philipp Harper
comments.body: The last thing Congress should do is authorize more money for the profligate fools in this administration to spend on a war they never should have started. Now, if Congress wants instead to earmark however many billions for the defense of Ukraine, including a resupply of Patriots, well, that’s a different story.

articles.summary: Ballot Initiative 195 would replace the flat tax with high graduated rates.

comments.name: gilbert brown
comments.body: So exactly where does one get the idea 'billionaires don't pay any taxes'.? That's a myth perpetrated by the jealous masses.  Have they broken any tax laws?  If they have, then the Feds would haul them in.  The Bernie crowd says a lot without any evidence.

comments.name: STUART MILLSTONE
comments.body: Power and control that's what Democrats want in general and progressive specifically. Move money from the private sector to the public sector where the government can control things. The case of Colorado it comes down primarily to the citizens of Denver and Boulder, and they will rule over the rest of the state.

comments.name: Joseph Comfort
comments.body: “Their fair share” is never fair enough.

comments.name: EDWARD JAWER
comments.body: One of the most well known pieces of advice to young people starting out is to be financially responsabile. Almost no one would disagree, yet in trying to run a Country, nothing could be farther from the way we spend  more than we make, much much more!  If that isn't  responsible why are we doing it? We are doing it because doing nothing is easier that doing something. When pay day comes those living through it will find a diffderent way of life. More different that be imagined! Lucky me, I'm 98.

comments.name: Rick T
comments.body: Yet another illustration of the Californication of Colorado.  When we left in the late '90s (because Denver was growing so fast - exploding costs of living, more crime, absurd traffic, overcrowded schools) they were swarming in like locusts, bringing their left-coast 'progressivism' with them.  Behold the fruits of California in-migration.

comments.name: JOHN PLAUCHE
comments.body: You have to hand it to the left wing PR geniuses that got the media to adopt the modern phrase "Progressive" for what in reality is just good old fashioned Socialist/Communist.

comments.name: Jeff S
comments.body: Colorado continues its mob democracy assault of the majority on the minority. What strikes me most, as a psychiatrist in practice for four decades, is who’s missing from this conversation: the doctor. Not the doctor as diagnostic vending machine — Choi mentions a “two-for-one sale” on assessments, which tells you what that encounter was — but the physician who knows you over time.

A diagnosis was never meant to be a transaction, still less a self-service one. It emerges from a relationship: a clinician who has seen you across seasons and setbacks, who knows your family and your patterns, who can say “this is new for you” or “you’ve weathered this before.” That longitudinal knowledge is the actual diagnostic instrument; the checklist is only its shorthand.

And we should be honest about why that doctor vanished. Not a shortage of physicians but a system that made the relationship impossible: 15-minute visits, prior authorizations, panels too large to know anyone, continuity destroyed by network churn. We industrialized medicine into throughput, then acted surprised when patients turned to an algorithm that at least pretends to know them — cold reading at scale, the fairground palm reader with better distribution.

What people seek in these labels — to be recognized, witnessed, given permission to be kind to themselves — is what the trusted clinical relationship once provided.  - diagnosis without it is a vacant label  We have lost the therapeutic alliance at the core of healthcare - without it , diagnosis is a meaningless illusion

comments.name: michael smolker
comments.body: Self-immolation is actually not such a foreign or unfathomable idea. One thing though is for sure: it comes from a place of profound determination. Not too many years ago, a janitor at the University of Washington, where I work, self-immolated in a very public way. Apparently he was deeply frustrated with the university's callous (putting it politely here) treatment of his cohort in their on again off again contract negotiations. This was at about the time that my unit had formed a labor union and we were in the process of negotiating our first contract. It took us almost 3 years (!!! )for us to get that first contract. I certainly don't mean to be flippant or to belittle this act, but let's just say that self-immolation crossed my mind a few times back then, as somebody who had worked for the university for already almost a quarter of a century without any labor protections. It is a statement of power of the powerless. That said, if this appeals in any way to any reader, just get help, talk to someone, especially a professional counselor.

When I was in school, there was no actual dress code. We did once wear our pajamas to breakfast - but it was at an off time and as a joke. And it was just the one time.

Usually we wore regular street clothes, beacuse the expectation was you left your room and grabbed your meal, then went out to class / into the wider world. 

However - it was an Ivy, and we heard stories about a time a few decades earlier when dinner required ties and jackets. That was a little different - ties and jackets (or the equivalent) would have been an added expense; regular street clothes would not have.

In general, I feel that the kids can wear what they want in their rooms. But "public" spaces are filled with people who you may run into later on a more professional basis. comments.name: Jacob P.
comments.body:
Always pleased to read about my own country in positive terms, as in this article. And in terms of hospitality, people coming to visit are most welcome.

But then there are second thoughts. Mass tourism often creates exactly the conditions people hope to escape from when they go on holiday: crowds, tension, noise, and a shortage of quiet or affordable places to stay. Amsterdam and Venice are classic examples of that paradox.

And then there are third thoughts. Mass tourism is not all that ancient. Half a century ago, the tourism industry was a trickle compared with the tsunami we see today. The numbers are illustrative. International tourism grew from about 222 million arrivals in 1975 to roughly 1.5 billion in 2025. Tourist air travel increased by almost 840%, while the cruise industry expanded by around 3,000%. 50 Years of Tourism: 1975–2025

All of this leaves a substantial footprint on what were once pristine and picturesque destinations, and on ecological health worldwide.

So, pleased as I am with this positive review of The Hague, it is worrying as well. I welcome each and every individual who wants to visit my country. It is just that there are so very many individuals. That’s the quirky part.

I hope the people of The Hague will forgive me when I say that there are even better places to be found in the Netherlands.

Originally Riche Mont, after one of William's strongholds in Normandy, the castle is the best surviving early Norman castle in England and is featured in The Domesday Book, William's inventory of his conquest. The town and the area are steeped in history from the Conquest on. And it happens to be the town where I was born, tho' nobody need go there on that account! Richmond, Yorkshire, would be an excellent diversion for visitors on the inevitable trip from York to Edinburgh.

By the way, Richmond upon Thames is one of the 57 other Richmonds named after the Yorkshire original.

To all the commenters who are bringing up the stereotype of dark wood floors showing dust more than light colored floors - I have to say that this not than my experience at all with dark wood floors! 

I have dark wood floors and have found them to be very practical and lovely to live with. 

I also have light colored wood floors.

Both dark and light wood floors need to be cleaned regularly or they both show lint and dust pretty much equally IMO. 

However, I have found that my light wood floors reflect drops of coffee or drops of food or lint MUCH more than the dark wood floors. Pet stains are much more visible on light wood floors. Much. Dust isn’t really the issue. It’s spills and crumbs that show up much more on light wood floors. 

Both dark and light colored wood floors need to be cleaned regularly or they just don’t look good.  No difference.

Don’t believe the stereotype!  If you like dark wood floors they are a joy to live with IMO.

Thank you to the firefighters. 

Both my grandfathers were firefighters. It was a tough job. This is back in the day when they wore metal hats and were called firemen. There were not smoke detectors in homes so they fought fires regularly. 

The job fed their families. My parents, with college degrees, did not need to work manually like their dads. They pursued the American dream of clean, cool work in offices. 

But what children want to forget, grandchildren will remember. I am a middle aged woman with a college education and years working in neat and tidy jobs finding that I am also just as much a firefighter as my grandpas. 

Not literally. I'm not employed by a firehouse. But for the last twenty years, since I saw An Inconvenient Truth, I've wanted to put out this greatest of all fires, this ever growing climate crisis. 

I've insulated my house, put on solar panels, gotten an entry level EV and charger in my garage and an efficient heat pump to heat and cool my small home. I make only a modest income but was able to piece together tax credits and rebates to do this. I rarely eat meat. I wear my clothes til they've got holes then wear them more in the garden. Never waste food. Compost. Fly about once every five years. 

I'm planting native shrubs, flowers, and trees in my small yard for the pollinators and birds. The loss of biodiversity is a twin crisis to climate change. It gives me hope to see neighbors do the same. 

May we all summon the courage to be firefighters.

comments.body: In my career as an officer of  Fortune 100 companies, I worked with many chiefs of staff. The simple description is a consigliere to the CEO, a role popularly associated with a Mafia family boss. As the author states, it isn't about logistical issues; that is the role of an executive assistant. It is being a sounding board, helping to think through or "war game" issues, getting feedback from peers (the COS is typically on the leadership team), and facilitating teamwork. There is nuance in this. Managing consultant-type skills are a great asset so long as the COS has some knowledge of the business. Unlike management consultancy, often hired to advance the cause of the company sponsor and therefore not trusted, the COS must walk a fine line between facilitation and information gathering to maintain the trust of peers. If that doesn't happen, the emperor continues to undress while all those around him, including the COF, compliment him (or her) on their attire. Loyalty in the corporate world is a team-based concept, and without it, the future is bleak.

I have a family history of heart disease.  It wasn't until my mid 50s I was put on a statin and within a year my blood glucose started rising. Within a few years I was put on BP medicine. In my early 60s, when I reported being fatigued I was asked if I ever had a stress test (I had not) yet the doctor did not order a test.  Move ahead a few years, after my doctor retired and I was assigned a new one, I reported shortness of breath. He did not order any further work up.  Two months later I had a heart attack and emergency quadruple bypass. All this to say is that we need to educate younger women about heart disease and how to deal with doctors who are asleep at the wheel.  When I had my first follow-up visit after my heart attack, all I could say to my doctor was  "What were you thinking? I could not have avoided bypass surgery but I could have avoided a heart attack." and rattled off my family history and a list of symptoms that should have warranted a full workup or at least a referral to a cardiologist.

My cardiologist wants me to lift weights more because although I'm not obese, I have a blob body type which because I'm in menopause and on a beta blocker, I could make me pre-diabetic. comments.body:
Recursive AI? Isn't that a giant leap toward self-improving intelligence?

The very act of recursive AI pushes it toward agency. Once given an objective, it can repeatedly evaluate its own results, revise its approach, and try again without waiting for human input. That's not much different from how AI helps debug code today—except the entire process becomes autonomous. Instead of a person saying, "That didn't work, try again," the AI determines that for itself and keeps iterating until it achieves its goal.

That's exactly why this new venture is so significant. These researchers are leaving the constraints of a large corporation because smaller, independent teams can move faster, take bigger risks, and iterate without layers of bureaucracy slowing them down.

Google is supporting the effort because it likely gets the first opportunity to capitalize on any breakthrough, potentially allowing it to leap ahead of the competition if the gamble pays off.

The potential breakthroughs from recursive AI are enormous, but so are the risks. Once an AI can repeatedly improve itself, each generation could become harder for humans to fully understand or control. I remain skeptical that human oversight alone would be enough if a truly autonomous recursive system were ever break from its leash.

Some thoughts on Tarot and divination:

Divination has been around for millennia. Card decks are at least as old as 9th century China (probably older). It's not much of a reach to consider that card decks were used for divination, even before the earliest and famous Tarot decks.

With respect to how Tarot might work, I'd suggest that it works in a similar way to the I Ching. Randomized outcomes of coin throws in that case lead to a "look-up" kind of index that when read or heard by a reader may help the reader or listener to find their own answers in their own minds.  I think the power of Tarot is in the same mechanism---the draw and layout of the drawn cards , navigated by someone familiar with the cards, helps the person whose "fortune" is being told sort out their own answers. I think there's a strong connection here with Jungian archetypes.

No one can tell the future; what one can do is try to sort out the present and its past.

Hannah, thank you for sharing this heartwarming and thought-provoking article this morning.

I've been fortunate to travel extensively through rural Japan since 2017. From Asahikawa to Kagoshima, I've found the people in these small Japanese villages to be consistently proud, hardworking, and deeply (even fiercely) committed to their way of life.

As a result, I have found that many of these communities have been slow to embrace change and are, quite visibly, aging. The effects of decades of rural depopulation and declining birthrates are impossible to miss. As a frequent visitor from America, I've found the contrast both striking and, at times, honestly sobering.

So it doesn't surprise me that many older residents in rural Japan are hesitant about robots and new technologies. More broadly, they tend to be cautious about change of any kind — including the sudden, unexpected arrival of an American "Gaijin" like me into their small villages.

Sadly, with Japan's fertility rate hovering around 1.2 children per woman and the long-standing reluctance of the LDP to significantly expand immigration, I worry that many rural communities will continue to fade. Over time, I fear that nature will gradually reclaim abandoned rice paddies, and the forests — and the bears that inhabit them — will once again dominate landscapes that had been farmed for generations.

It's located in a beautifully restored 400 seat theater on the second floor of town hall. It has state of the art projection (both digital and film) and live local music before each screening.

comments.name: Average Hoosier
comments.body: College Theater, Storrs, CT, UConn campus. 800 seats, big speakers, velvet curtains, features were three days and four days, Hollywood's Second Golden Age. I was a bozo-haired usher in tux with flashlight. The manager was from RKO in Boston, totally old school. My future wife sold pre-p0pped popcorn. Just marvelous! I went on to film studies in college and near poverty after. The megaplex, sterile theaters today pale in comparison. I guess only the French still hold cinema as religion and un certain regard.

comments.name: KC
comments.body: Speaking of Schoenbrun's media focused art, she has a novel releasing in October titled "Public Access Afterworld" that originated as a television series she couldn't get picked up. I got an ARC of the novel, and it was fantastic, and had her usual hallmarks: identity through media, a sense of otherness, and trans identity. If you have enjoyed any of her films, you should definitely check it out when it releases.
